content: Double volume exchange transfusion is a standard treatment for newborns with severe jaundice, primarily to prevent kernicterus and other toxic effects associated with high bilirubin levels. This procedure is most frequently performed in infants suffering from rhesus hemolytic disease. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness of single volume exchange transfusion (SVET) and double volume exchange transfusion (DVET) in achieving survival without disability and in reducing bilirubin levels in newborns with severe jaundice. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and SCISEARCH, up until March 2006. Additionally, reference lists from identified articles and review papers were examined, and unpublished data were sought through personal communication with experts in the field. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that directly compared single volume and double volume exchange transfusions in jaundiced newborns. The safety and efficacy of these two approaches were assessed in terms of long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, reduction in bilirubin levels, and complications during the exchange transfusion process. Data were analyzed separately based on the underlying cause of jaundice. For dichotomous variables, relative risk (RR) was calculated, while weighted mean difference (WMD) was used for continuous variables. A fixed-effects model was applied, and 95% confidence intervals were reported. Only one study, conducted by Amato in 1988, met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 20 full-term infants who required exchange transfusion due to hemolytic jaundice caused by ABO incompatibility. These infants were randomly assigned to receive either single volume or double volume exchange transfusion. The baseline characteristics of the two groups were comparable, including birth weight (3260 ± 390 g vs. 3350 ± 410 g), gestational age (39 ± 1 weeks vs. 40 ± 0.8 weeks), and pre-exchange bilirubin levels (199 ± 33 µmol/L vs. 216 ± 55 µmol/L). Both groups received identical treatment protocols, except for the volume of blood used during the exchange transfusion. The study found no significant difference in total bilirubin levels immediately after the exchange transfusion between the two groups. However, no long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed in this study. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of single volume exchange transfusion as an alternative to double volume exchange transfusion in jaundiced newborns. Based on the current evidence, it is not recommended to deviate from the standard practice of using double volume exchange transfusions for severe neonatal jaundice.
